title: Does AI Help You Learn—or Just Finish?

adaptation.scope: Full argument adaptation; not a three-minute abridgment. Natural speech determines final runtime.
preserved: Assisted, independent, retention and transfer distinctions
Turkish three-arm experiment and statistical limits
Harvard physics and checked mathematics-help counterexamples
Retrieval with feedback, worked examples and attempt-before-instruction evidence
Adaptive guidance and independent transfer/retention checks

claims.claim: Assisted performance, independent performance, delayed retention and transfer are different outcomes. Current fluency does not establish durable unaided knowledge.
claims.verification: Official research overview retrieved live on 2026-10-22. Used for distinctions and fluency; no new numerical effect claimed.

claims.claim: Bastani et al.: nearly 1,000 high-school mathematics students in Turkey; GPT Base raised practice grades by 48% relative to control but reduced subsequent unassisted exam grades by 17%.
claims.verification: Author PDF retrieved live on 2026-10-22; abstract and page 10 directly verified. These are relative changes, not percentage points. Assessment is short term. Script avoids treating publication year as experiment year.

claims.claim: GPT Tutor used teacher-prepared material and hints; practice grades rose 127% relative to control. Its unassisted exam result was statistically indistinguishable from control.
claims.verification: Fresh author PDF page 10 confirms non-significant guarded-tutor exam result. Lack of statistical significance is not proof of identical outcomes. Interaction logs inform interpretation but do not isolate all mediators.

claims.claim: Kestin et al.: an instructor-designed AI tutor improved immediate college physics post-test scores relative to active classroom instruction; medians 4.5 and 3.5 respectively.
claims.verification: Publisher full text retrieved live on 2026-10-22. Harvard N=194; pooled post-test observations differ by condition. Results section directly verifies medians, immediate testing, structured content, questions and feedback. No long-delay claim.

claims.claim: Cognitive offloading changes information-processing requirements through an external aid. Its practical value depends on the task and target process.
claims.verification: UCL author record and abstract retrieved live on 2026-10-22. Learning advice in the film is editorial application, not a direct effect size from this review.

claims.claim: Worked examples improved immediate retention and near-transfer tests relative to unguided problem solving for 114 novice Year-7 students learning bracket expansion in Indonesia.
claims.verification: Direct DOI fetch returned 403; current publisher-indexed full text retrieved via search on 2026-10-22, including Methods and Procedure. Tests immediately followed learning; the paper calls one retention but that is not delayed retention.

claims.claim: A 44-study meta-analysis compared retrieval practice with elaborative learning activities; relative benefits were moderated by comparator and corrective feedback.
claims.verification: Publisher abstract retrieved live on 2026-10-22: 142 comparisons, small overall advantage, feedback moderation. Script omits effect sizes and does not claim recall is universally best.

claims.claim: A 2026 randomized middle-school mathematics working paper with more than 6,000 students tested AI support, mastery progression and a one-week assessment. Delayed benefits were limited and conditional.
claims.verification: Author-deposited abstract retrieved live on 2026-10-22. Hamilton County Schools, NUMI platform, practiced and unpracticed material. Most encouraging delayed result was marginally significant and concentrated on practiced Exercise 1 with mastery. Not presented as a general significant gain.

claims.claim: A preregistered study of 704 adults using an assistant for fraction arithmetic found metacognitive feedback reduced complete-answer requests and improved a subsequent unaided test; researchers found no evidence that effort rewards affected either outcome.
claims.verification: Current arXiv abstract retrieved live on 2026-10-22 directly verifies N=704, preregistration, task, feedback and reward findings. Script retains preprint and task limitations and does not convert odds ratios into percentage changes in probability.

claims.claim: Pardos and Bhandari randomized 274 participants across mathematics topics. Generated help improved learning relative to no help; the AI-human help difference was not significant. Initial generated help failed quality checks on 32% of problems.
claims.verification: Publisher full text retrieved live on 2026-10-22. Abstract and Results verify design and 32% initial quality failures; these are generated worked-solution hints, not an unrestricted Socratic-chat intervention. Script does not claim exact equivalence.

claims.claim: A meta-analysis of 53 studies favored problem solving followed by instruction overall, with age, task and implementation moderators.
claims.verification: Publisher DOI timed out; author institutional repository PDF and ETH publication record retrieved via current search on 2026-10-22. 53 studies and 166 comparisons. Not evidence for a universal chatbot prompting rule.

claims.claim: Late-night spreadsheet, learner and next-morning failure are invented illustrative scenarios, not real study participants.
Name the skill, select suitable help, reconstruct with the answer hidden, check, vary the problem, and return later: an editorial synthesis, not a separately validated protocol or prescribed timing.
Original algebra illustration: 2(x+3)=14 gives x=4; expansion is 2x+6, not 2x+3. Near-transfer example 3(y-2)=15 gives y=7.
claims.verification: Direct substitution: 2(4+3)=14 and 3(7-2)=15. Both operations applied to both sides.
